        }
        else if (iy == 0){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iy == DATAYSIZE-1){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iz == 0){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iz == DATAZSIZE-1){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void swapGrid(double cnew[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
              double cold[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE])
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {
        double tmp = cnew[ix][iy][iz];
        cnew[ix][iy][iz] = cold[ix][iy][iz];
        cold[ix][iy][iz] = tmp;
      }
    }
  }
}

void initializationPhi(double phi[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE], double r0)
{
  #pragma omp parallel for collapse(3)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {
        double r = std::sqrt(SQ(ix-0.5*DATAXSIZE) + SQ(iy-0.5*DATAYSIZE) + SQ(iz-0.5*DATAZSIZE));
        if (r < r0){
          phi[ix][iy][iz] = 1.0;
        }
        else
        {
          phi[ix][iy][iz] = -1.0;
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void initializationU(double u[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE], double r0, double delta)
{
  #pragma omp parallel for collapse(3)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {
        double r = std::sqrt(SQ(ix-0.5*DATAXSIZE) + SQ(iy-0.5*DATAYSIZE) + SQ(iz-0.5*DATAZSIZE));
        if (r < r0) {
          u[ix][iy][iz] = 0.0;
        }
        else
        {
          u[ix][iy][iz] = -delta * (1.0 - std::exp(-(r-r0)));
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
  const int num_steps = atoi(argv[1]);  //6000;
  const double dx = 0.4;
  const double dy = 0.4;
  const double dz = 0.4;
  const double dt = 0.01;
  const double delta = 0.8;
  const double r0 = 5.0;
  const double epsilon = 0.07;
  const double W0 = 1.0;
  const double beta0 = 0.0;
  const double D = 2.0;
  const double d0 = 0.5;
  const double a1 = 1.25 / std::sqrt(2.0);
  const double a2 = 0.64;
  const double lambda = (W0*a1)/(d0);
  const double tau0 = ((W0*W0*W0*a1*a2)/(d0*D)) + ((W0*W0*beta0)/(d0));

  // overall data set sizes
  const int nx = DATAXSIZE;
  const int ny = DATAYSIZE;
  const int nz = DATAZSIZE;
  const int vol = nx * ny * nz;
  const size_t vol_in_bytes = sizeof(double) * vol;

  // storage for result stored on host
  nRarray *phi_host = (nRarray *)malloc(vol_in_bytes);
  nRarray *u_host = (nRarray *)malloc(vol_in_bytes);
  initializationPhi(phi_host,r0);
  initializationU(u_host,r0,delta);

#ifdef VERIFY
  nRarray *phi_ref = (nRarray *)malloc(vol_in_bytes);
  nRarray *u_ref = (nRarray *)malloc(vol_in_bytes);
  memcpy(phi_ref, phi_host, vol_in_bytes);
  memcpy(u_ref, u_host, vol_in_bytes);
  reference(phi_ref, u_ref, vol, num_steps);
#endif

  auto offload_start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

  // storage for result computed on device
  double *d_phiold = (double*)phi_host;
  double *d_uold = (double*)u_host;
  double *d_phinew = (double*) malloc (vol_in_bytes);
  double *d_unew = (double*) malloc (vol_in_bytes);
  double *d_Fx = (double*) malloc (vol_in_bytes);
  double *d_Fy = (double*) malloc (vol_in_bytes);
  double *d_Fz = (double*) malloc (vol_in_bytes);

  #pragma omp target data map(tofrom: d_phiold[0:vol], \
                                      d_uold[0:vol]) \
                          map(alloc: d_phinew[0:vol], \
                                     d_unew[0:vol], \
                                     d_Fx[0:vol],\
                                     d_Fy[0:vol],\
                                     d_Fz[0:vol])
  {
    int t = 0;

    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    while (t <= num_steps) {

      calculateForce((nRarray*)d_phiold, (nRarray*)d_Fx,(nRarray*)d_Fy,(nRarray*)d_Fz,
                     dx,dy,dz,epsilon,W0,tau0);

      allenCahn((nRarray*)d_phinew,(nRarray*)d_phiold,(nRarray*)d_uold,
                (nRarray*)d_Fx,(nRarray*)d_Fy,(nRarray*)d_Fz,
                epsilon,W0,tau0,lambda, dt,dx,dy,dz);

      boundaryConditionsPhi((nRarray*)d_phinew);

      thermalEquation((nRarray*)d_unew,(nRarray*)d_uold,(nRarray*)d_phinew,(nRarray*)d_phiold,
                      D,dt,dx,dy,dz);

      boundaryConditionsU((nRarray*)d_unew,delta);

      swapGrid((nRarray*)d_phinew, (nRarray*)d_phiold);

      swapGrid((nRarray*)d_unew, (nRarray*)d_uold);

      t++;
    }

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Total kernel execution time: %.3f (ms)\n", time * 1e-6f);
  }

  auto offload_end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
  auto offload_time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(offload_end - offload_start).count();
  printf("Offload time: %.3f (ms)\n", offload_time * 1e-6f);

#ifdef VERIFY
  bool ok = true;
  for (int idx = 0; idx < nx; idx++)
    for (int idy = 0; idy < ny; idy++)
      for (int idz = 0; idz < nz; idz++) {
        if (fabs(phi_ref[idx][idy][idz] - phi_host[idx][idy][idz]) > 1e-3) {
          ok = false; printf("phi: %lf %lf\n", phi_ref[idx][idy][idz], phi_host[idx][idy][idz]);
	}
        if (fabs(u_ref[idx][idy][idz] - u_host[idx][idy][idz]) > 1e-3) {
          ok = false; printf("u: %lf %lf\n", u_ref[idx][idy][idz], u_host[idx][idy][idz]);
        }
      }
  printf("%s\n", ok ? "PASS" : "FAIL");
  free(phi_ref);
  free(u_ref);
#endif

  free(phi_host);
  free(u_host);
  free(d_phinew);
  free(d_unew);
  free(d_Fx);
  free(d_Fy);
  free(d_Fz);
  return 0;
}

double dFphi(double phi, double u, double lambda)
{

}


double GradientX(double phi[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
                 double dx, double dy, double dz, int x, int y, int z)
{
  return (phi[x+1][y][z] - phi[x-1][y][z]) / (2.0*dx);
}


double GradientY(double phi[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],

double GradientZ(double phi[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],

  double phiyy = (phi[x][y+1][z] + phi[x][y-1][z] - 2.0 * phi[x][y][z]) / SQ(dy);
  double phizz = (phi[x][y][z+1] + phi[x][y][z-1] - 2.0 * phi[x][y][z]) / SQ(dz);

void thermalEquation(double unew[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
                     double uold[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
                     double phinew[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
                     double phiold[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
                     double D, double dt, double dx, double dy, double dz)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)
  for (int ix = 1; ix < DATAXSIZE-1; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 1; iy < DATAYSIZE-1; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 1; iz < DATAZSIZE-1; iz++) {

        unew[ix][iy][iz] = uold[ix][iy][iz] +
          0.5*(phinew[ix][iy][iz]-
               phiold[ix][iy][iz]) +
          dt * D * Laplacian(uold,dx,dy,dz,ix,iy,iz);
      }
    }
  }
}

void boundaryConditionsU(double unew[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE], double delta)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {

        if (ix == 0){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (ix == DATAXSIZE-1){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iy == 0){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iy == DATAYSIZE-1){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iz == 0){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
        else if (iz == DATAZSIZE-1){
          unew[ix][iy][iz] =  -delta;
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void swapGrid(double cnew[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE],
              double cold[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE])
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {
        double tmp = cnew[ix][iy][iz];
        cnew[ix][iy][iz] = cold[ix][iy][iz];
        cold[ix][iy][iz] = tmp;
      }
    }
  }
}

void initializationPhi(double phi[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE], double r0)
{
  #pragma omp parallel for collapse(3)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {
        double r = std::sqrt(SQ(ix-0.5*DATAXSIZE) + SQ(iy-0.5*DATAYSIZE) + SQ(iz-0.5*DATAZSIZE));
        if (r < r0){
          phi[ix][iy][iz] = 1.0;
        }
        else
        {
          phi[ix][iy][iz] = -1.0;
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void initializationU(double u[][DATAYSIZE][DATAZSIZE], double r0, double delta)
{
  #pragma omp parallel for collapse(3)
  for (int ix = 0; ix < DATAXSIZE; ix++) {
    for (int iy = 0; iy < DATAYSIZE; iy++) {
      for (int iz = 0; iz < DATAZSIZE; iz++) {
        double r = std::sqrt(SQ(ix-0.5*DATAXSIZE) + SQ(iy-0.5*DATAYSIZE) + SQ(iz-0.5*DATAZSIZE));
        if (r < r0) {
          u[ix][iy][iz] = 0.0;
        }
        else
        {
          u[ix][iy][iz] = -delta * (1.0 - std::exp(-(r-r0)));
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

  const double dx = 0.4;
  const double dy = 0.4;
  const double dz = 0.4;
  const double dt = 0.01;
  const double delta = 0.8;

metrics_explanations.fp64_flop_explanation: The kernel only evaluates integer equality comparisons on ix/iy/iz against 0 or 399 and conditionally stores the constant -1.0 to phinew; there is no double arithmetic such as add/mul/div/sub/neg on data values in the kernel body. Treating comparisons on integers as non-FP and constant stores as non-FLOP gives zero FP64 FLOPs for the first invocation.
metrics_explanations.fp16_flop_explanation: The kernel uses no half-precision data or arithmetic, and there is no evidence from source that the compiler would generate packed FP16 helper arithmetic for this simple constant-store kernel. Thus the FP16 FLOP count is estimated as zero.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel does not read phinew or any other global array; it only uses loop indices and writes boundary cells. Because all control decisions are based on indices, there is effectively no global-memory read footprint attributable to this kernel invocation.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Only boundary points of the 400^3 array are written: total boundary cells = 400^3 - 398^3 = 955,208, each storing one 8-byte double, for 7,641,664 bytes of unique stores. This unique write footprint exceeds the 5 MB L2 cache, so during the first invocation dirty lines will be evicted and the best DRAM-write estimate is the unique boundary-store footprint.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The thermalEquation kernel iterates over ix=1..398, iy=1..398, iz=1..398, giving 398*398*398 = 63,044,792 iterations. The SASS shows the grid uses a stride pattern with blockSz=256. The total iteration space is 63,044,792. Looking at the SASS, the comparison at offset 0x0040 checks R49 > 0x3c1fc = 246268. The iteration count encoded is 0x3c1fcb8 = 63,044,792 at offset 0x0a60. The grid is launched with ceil(63044792/256) = 246269 blocks, but the SASS guard at 0x0040 uses 0x3c1fc = 246268 (0-indexed), so gridSz.x = 246269. However, OpenMP runtime may choose a different grid size; the SASS outer loop at 0x0a00-0x0a90 shows a grid-stride loop where R0 = c[0x0][0xc] (gridDim.x) is used to stride. The initial check at 0x0040 compares CTAID.X > 0x3c1fc, and the stride loop at 0x0a60 checks if R49 >= 0x3c1fcb8. This is consistent with a runtime-chosen grid size. For OpenMP on clang with sm_86, a common choice is to use enough blocks to cover the iteration space, so gridSz = [246269, 1, 1].

For each active thread (63,044,792 iterations), the kernel reads from 4 arrays: uold, phinew, phiold (with stencil neighbors), and the center values.

From the SASS LDG instructions per iteration:
1. R22+0x271c88: phi[x+1][y][z] from uold (8 bytes)
2. R22+0xc88: phi[x-1][y][z] from uold (8 bytes)  
3. R22+0x139488: uold[x][y][z] center (8 bytes)
4. R8+0x139488: phinew[x][y][z] (8 bytes)
5. R10+0x139488: phiold[x][y][z] (8 bytes)
6. R22+0x13a108: uold[x][y+1][z] (8 bytes)
7. R22+0x138808: uold[x][y-1][z] (8 bytes)
8. R22+0x139490: uold[x][y][z+1] (8 bytes)
9. R22+0x139480: uold[x][y][z-1] (8 bytes)

That's 9 loads × 8 bytes = 72 bytes per thread. But due to stencil overlap, the unique footprint for uold is 400×400×400×8 = 512,000,000 bytes (the full array since we access interior points and their neighbors). For phinew and phiold, we access only center values at interior points: 398×398×398×8 bytes each = 504,358,336 bytes each.

Total unique read footprint: uold (512MB) + phinew (~504MB) + phiold (~504MB) ≈ 1,520,716,672 bytes. This far exceeds the 5MB L2 cache, so most reads will come from DRAM. The stencil reuse in uold means some neighbor accesses hit cache lines already loaded, reducing traffic. For a 3D stencil with 7-point access pattern on uold, the unique footprint is ~512MB. With cache line size of 128 bytes (16 doubles), there's significant spatial reuse along the z-dimension.

For uold: unique footprint ≈ 400×400×400×8 = 512,000,000 bytes
For phinew: 398×398×398×8 = 504,358,336 bytes  
For phiold: 398×398×398×8 = 504,358,336 bytes

Total unique read footprint ≈ 1,520,716,672 bytes. Given the working set far exceeds L2, DRAM reads ≈ unique footprint ≈ 1,520,716,672 bytes.

The write footprint is 504,358,336 bytes, which will mostly go to DRAM.

prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: The kernel only stores the constant -1.0 to boundary elements. The unary negation of 1.0 to produce -1.0 is a compile-time constant, not a runtime FP64 operation. There are no runtime FP64 arithmetic operations — only stores of a pre-computed constant. Thus FP64 FLOPs = 0.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: There are no half-precision operations in the source code. The compiler may insert a small number of HFMA2 instructions for constant/zero materialization, but without SASS evidence, we conservatively estimate 0 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel only writes to boundary elements (where ix==0, ix==399, iy==0, iy==399, iz==0, or iz==399) and does not read any array data — it only stores the constant -1.0. However, for write-allocate cache policy, the GPU must read the cache lines before writing to them. The number of boundary elements: the 6 faces of a 400×400×400 cube minus overlaps. Total boundary elements = 400^3 - 398^3 = 64,000,000 - 63,044,792 = 955,208 elements. Each element is 8 bytes, so the boundary write footprint is ~7,641,664 bytes. Due to write-allocate, the GPU reads these cache lines from DRAM first. However, the array phinew is 64M elements × 8 bytes = 512 MB, which far exceeds the 5 MB L2 cache. The boundary elements are scattered across the array (face elements at various ix, iy, iz positions). For the ix==0 and ix==399 faces, these are contiguous blocks of 400×400×8 = 1,280,000 bytes each. For iy and iz boundary faces, elements are strided. The write-allocate reads would be approximately equal to the written footprint. Estimating ~7,641,664 bytes read from DRAM for write-allocate.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes -1.0 to all boundary elements of the 400×400×400 array. The boundary elements are those where any of ix, iy, iz equals 0 or 399. The total number of boundary elements is 400^3 - 398^3 = 955,208. Each is 8 bytes (double), so the total written data is 955,208 × 8 = 7,641,664 bytes. Since the full array is 512 MB which far exceeds the 5 MB L2 cache, the written cache lines will be evicted to DRAM as the kernel progresses through the iteration space. The boundary writes are spread across the entire array address range, so L2 evictions will occur. DRAM bytes written ≈ 7,641,664 bytes.

- R10+0x139488: uold[x][y-1][z] (via different base)

- R22+0x139490, R22+0x139480: phinew[x][y][z], phiold[x][y][z] (or uold[x][y][z+1] and uold[x][y][z-1])

prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel only writes phinew boundary elements and performs no global loads from phinew or other arrays in SASS; control uses indices and constants only. Hence there is no DRAM read traffic attributable to kernel data accesses in the first invocation.

args.blockSz_explanation: `thread_limit(256)` on the collapsed OpenMP target loop is the only explicit bound on per-team threads. LLVM OpenMP offload typically uses a 1-D CUDA block for such kernels, so the defensible estimate is blockSz = [256,1,1].
args.fp32_flop_explanation: All floating-point work in the kernel source is in double precision (`double`), and there are no float or half variables or operations in the executed path. Therefore the source-based FP32 count for the first invocation is zero.
args.fp64_flop_explanation: The kernel executes over all 64,000,000 collapsed iterations, but only the interior 398^3 = 63,044,792 points take the heavy path; boundary points only store zeros. Per interior point: GradientX/Y/Z cost 3×(1 subtraction + 1 multiply for `2.0*dx` + 1 division)=9 FLOPs; `sqGphi` adds 3 squares + 2 adds =5; `c=16*W0*epsilon` =2; `Wn` includes `An`, where the nonzero branch is taken here because initialized phi is ±1 so interior gradients near the initial sphere are sparse but for a source-level estimate we conservatively count the executed expression when computing w: `An` costs 3*(square+square)=6, numerator sums 2 adds, denominator has 3 squares +2 adds done twice plus 1 multiply, ratio 1 div, scale terms about 6 more ops, total 21; then Wn adds 1 multiply; `w2` square =1. Each `dFunc` call on the nonzero-expression path costs 3 cubes as 6 muls, four squares 4 muls, two fourth-powers via square-of-square 2 muls, numerator combination 6 ops, denominator 7 ops including final division, total 25; three calls give 75. Each output assignment `w2*phi? + sqGphi*w*c*dFunc(...)` costs 4 multiplies + 1 add =5, done 3 times gives 15. Total per interior point = 9+5+2+21+1+1+75+15 = 129 FP64 FLOPs; boundaries do 0 FP arithmetic. Thus total FP64 FLOPs = 63,044,792 × 129 = 8,132,778,168. This is source-level and may differ if the compiler hoists/reuses subexpressions inside inlined helpers.
args.fp16_flop_explanation: The kernel uses only `double` arrays, constants, and helper functions, with no half-precision data or source-level half arithmetic. Without SASS evidence of compiler-generated packed half instructions, the conservative FP16 count is zero.
args.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The arrays are much larger than the 5 MB L2, so cache cannot retain the full working set; for the first invocation of `calculateForce`, reads are dominated by the source loads from `phi`. Each interior point evaluates GradientX/Y/Z, reading 6 neighboring doubles total, and the boundary path does no phi reads; with 63,044,792 interior points this gives 6 × 8 bytes × 63,044,792 = 3,026,150,016 bytes read from DRAM as a streaming estimate. This ignores any modest cache-line sharing among neighboring threads because the footprint (512 MB for phi) is far larger than L2 and the access pattern is stencil-like but effectively streaming at this scale.
args.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Every one of the 64,000,000 iterations writes three doubles, either computed force values for interior points or zeros on the boundary, so total store traffic is 64,000,000 × 3 × 8 = 1,536,000,000 bytes. The combined unique write footprint across Fx/Fy/Fz is also 1.536 GB, far exceeding the 5 MB L2, so dirty lines will be evicted during the kernel and essentially all of this store traffic reaches DRAM during the invocation.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel iterates over a 400×400×400 = 64,000,000 element space with thread_limit(256). The SASS shows a grid-stride loop pattern where each block processes 256 elements per iteration, and the grid exit condition checks against 0x3d090 = 250000. The SASS compares CTAID.X against 0x3d08f (250,000-1), so the grid size is 250,000 blocks. This corresponds to 64,000,000 / 256 = 250,000.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The OpenMP directive specifies thread_limit(256), and the SASS shows thread-level operations consistent with 256 threads per block.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: No FP32 arithmetic operations are visible in the SASS for this kernel. The kernel only stores a double-precision constant (-1.0) to boundary elements. All address computations are integer.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, the only floating-point instruction is the STG.E.64 that stores the constant -1.0 (materialized as R10=0x0, R11=0xBFF00000). There are no DFMA, DMUL, DADD, or other FP64 arithmetic instructions. The kernel only writes a constant to boundary elements without any FP64 computation.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: No FP16 instructions are present in the SASS for this kernel. The kernel performs only integer address arithmetic and stores a double-precision constant.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: This kernel only writes to boundary elements; it does not read any global memory data (no LDG instructions in the SASS). The only reads are from constant memory (c[0x0][...]) for kernel arguments. There are no DRAM reads from the phinew array. Thus DRAM bytes read is 0.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes -1.0 (8 bytes, double) to all boundary elements of a 400×400×400 array. The boundary elements are: faces at ix=0, ix=399 (each 400×400=160,000), iy=0, iy=399 (each 398×400=159,200 excluding corners already counted), iz=0, iz=399 (each 398×398=158,404 excluding edges already counted). Total boundary elements = 2×160,000 + 2×159,200 + 2×158,404 = 320,000 + 318,400 + 316,808 = 955,208. Each write is 8 bytes, so total write footprint = 955,208 × 8 = 7,641,664 bytes. This is about 7.3 MB which exceeds the L2 cache size of 6 MB, so most writes will spill to DRAM. The write addresses are scattered across the 400×400×400 array (512 MB total), touching cache lines on the boundaries. The unique cache lines touched: for face ix=0 and ix=399, each is a contiguous 400×400×8 = 1,280,000 bytes region. For iy=0 and iy=399 faces, each row of 400 elements (3200 bytes) is separated by 400×8=3200 bytes stride. For iz=0 and iz=399, elements are separated by 3200 bytes. The total unique bytes written is 7,641,664 bytes. Since this exceeds L2 (6MB), DRAM writes ≈ 7,641,664 bytes. With write-allocate policy, cache lines need to be read before writing for partial-line writes, but most boundary writes are scattered, so we estimate DRAM writes ≈ 7,641,664 bytes.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The swapGrid kernel iterates over a 400×400×400 = 64,000,000 element space with `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)`. The total number of threads needed is 64,000,000. With a block size of 256, the grid size would be ceil(64,000,000/256) = 250,000. However, OpenMP runtimes on clang/LLVM for NVIDIA GPUs typically launch with a grid-stride loop pattern. A common heuristic is to use a number of teams equal to ceil(N/thread_limit) = 250,000, but the runtime may cap this. For clang's OpenMP offload targeting sm_80, the runtime typically launches enough teams to cover the iteration space, so gridSz = [250000, 1, 1].
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The thread_limit(256) clause in the pragma sets the block size to 256 threads. This gives blockSz = [256, 1, 1].
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: The swapGrid kernel only performs double-precision swaps (load, store) with no floating-point arithmetic at all. There are no FP32 operations in the kernel body. The compiler might insert a small number of FP32 helper instructions (e.g., for index computation), but these are integer operations, not FP32. So FP32 FLOPs = 0.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: The swapGrid kernel body is: tmp = cnew[ix][iy][iz]; cnew[ix][iy][iz] = cold[ix][iy][iz]; cold[ix][iy][iz] = tmp. This is purely load/store operations with no floating-point arithmetic. There are no FP64 operations. FP64 FLOPs = 0.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: There are no FP16 operations in this kernel. The kernel only swaps double-precision values. FP16 FLOPs = 0.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The swapGrid kernel reads from two arrays: cnew and cold. Each array has 400×400×400 = 64,000,000 double elements. Each thread reads one element from cnew (8 bytes) and one element from cold (8 bytes). Total unique read footprint = 2 × 64,000,000 × 8 = 1,024,000,000 bytes = ~1024 MB. The L2 cache is 40 MB, which is far smaller than the 1 GB read footprint, so essentially all reads must come from DRAM. DRAM bytes read ≈ 1,024,000,000 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The swapGrid kernel writes to both cnew and cold arrays. Each array has 64,000,000 doubles = 512,000,000 bytes. Total unique write footprint = 2 × 512,000,000 = 1,024,000,000 bytes. Since the write footprint (1024 MB) far exceeds the L2 cache (40 MB), the writes will be evicted from L2 to DRAM during the kernel execution. Additionally, since these are streaming writes to previously-read locations, the write-back traffic should be approximately equal to the unique write footprint. DRAM bytes written ≈ 1,024,000,000 bytes.

prediction.blockSz_explanation: The source directive uses `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)`, and the SASS confirms a 256-thread block via left shift by 8 bits when forming the per-CTA starting linear index. prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: There is no source-level FP32 arithmetic in `swapGrid`; all data are doubles and the SASS load/store path contains no FP32 math relevant to the swap. The lone `HFMA2.MMA` in SASS is compiler-generated control/materialization in FP16, not FP32.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Per swapped element, the source performs only three double assignments through a temporary (`tmp=cnew[...]`, `cnew[...] = cold[...]`, `cold[...] = tmp`) with no double arithmetic operations such as add/mul/div/negate. SASS confirms the taken path is two `LDG.E.64` plus two `STG.E.64` and address arithmetic only, so FP64 FLOPs are zero over all 64,000,000 elements.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: SASS contains one executed `HFMA2.MMA R12, -RZ, RZ, 0, 5.9604644775390625e-08` before entering the per-thread work loop; this is compiler-generated packed half arithmetic used to materialize a control value. It executes once per participating thread instance that reaches the work section, contributing 4 FP16 FLOPs each; with 250,000 blocks * 256 threads = 64,000,000 threads, that yields 256,000,000 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each of the 64,000,000 swapped elements causes two 8-byte global loads in SASS (`LDG.E.64` from `cnew` and `cold`) on the taken path. prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each element also causes two 8-byte global stores (`STG.E.64`) back to the two arrays, so total store traffic is 64,000,000 * 16 = 1,024,000,000 bytes. Breaking down the Laplacian function:
- phixx = (phi[x+1][y][z] + phi[x-1][y][z] - 2.0*phi[x][y][z]) / SQ(dx)
  = 1 add + 1 sub (or add of neg) + 1 mul (2.0*) + 1 div (or mul by reciprocal) = let me count carefully:
  - phi[x+1][y][z] + phi[x-1][y][z]: 1 FADD
  - 2.0 * phi[x][y][z]: 1 FMUL
  - subtract: 1 FADD (sub)
  - SQ(dx) = dx*dx: 1 FMUL
  - divide: 1 FDIV (but compiler likely precomputes 1/SQ(dx) and uses FMUL)
  So phixx: ~3-4 FP64 ops (add, mul, sub, mul_by_reciprocal). With FMA: could be 1 FMA + 1 add + 1 mul = effectively 3 ops, or the compiler may use DFMA to combine.

Let me count more carefully at the source level:
Laplacian:
- phixx: phi[x+1]+phi[x-1] (1 add), 2.0*phi[x][y][z] (1 mul), subtract (1 sub), /SQ(dx) where SQ(dx)=dx*dx is a constant precomputed. So divide by constant = 1 mul. Or: 1 add + 1 FMA + 1 mul = 4 flops.
- Similarly phiyy: 4 flops
- Similarly phizz: 4 flops
- phixx + phiyy: 1 add
- + phizz: 1 add
Total Laplacian: ~14 FP64 ops

- 0.5 * (phinew - phiold): 1 sub + 1 mul = 2 ops
- dt * D: precomputed constant = 0 ops at runtime (or 1 mul)
- dt*D * Laplacian: 1 mul
- uold + 0.5*(...): 1 add
- + dt*D*Laplacian: 1 add

- 0.5 * diff: 1 mul (or FMA)
- dt * D: 1 mul (likely hoisted)
- dtD * Laplacian: 1 mul
- uold + half_diff: 1 add
- + dtD_lap: 1 add
= 5 ops (if dt*D not hoisted) or 4 ops

phiyy: same → 4 ops  
phizz: same → 4 ops
sum: 2 adds → 2 ops

args.dram_bytes_read_explanation:
Each of the 63,044,792 interior threads reads from 4 arrays: uold (7 unique elements for the stencil: center + 6 neighbors), phinew (1 element), phiold (1 element). However, due to the 3D stencil pattern on uold, neighboring threads share many cache lines.

Unique data footprint:
- uold: The full interior + boundary halo = 400*400*400 doubles = 512,000,000 bytes. The stencil accesses x±1, y±1, z±1 neighbors, so essentially the entire array is touched.
- phinew: Interior points 398*398*398 = 63,044,792 * 8 = 504,358,336 bytes
- phiold: Interior points 398*398*398 = 63,044,792 * 8 = 504,358,336 bytes

Total unique read footprint: ~512,000,000 + 504,358,336 + 504,358,336 = ~1,520,716,672 bytes.

The L2 cache is 40 MB = 41,943,040 bytes. The total read footprint is ~1.52 GB, far exceeding L2. So most reads will go to DRAM.

For uold with the stencil pattern, each element is read by up to 7 threads but the unique footprint is ~400*400*400*8 = 512,000,000 bytes. With good spatial locality along z dimension (contiguous), cache reuse will help somewhat but the working set is too large for L2.

Total DRAM bytes read ≈ 512,000,000 + 504,358,336 + 504,358,336 = 1,520,716,672 bytes. Due to cache line granularity (128 bytes), there may be some overhead at row boundaries, but the arrays are contiguous so this is minimal.
args.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes to unew for each of the 63,044,792 interior points. Each write is 8 bytes (double). The unique write footprint is 63,044,792 * 8 = 504,358,336 bytes. This is ~504 MB, far exceeding the 40 MB L2 cache, so essentially all writes will be evicted to DRAM during the kernel execution. With write-back caching, the writes happen as cache lines are evicted. Given the streaming nature and large footprint, most written data will reach DRAM. Total DRAM bytes written ≈ 504,358,336 bytes. Due to write-allocate policy, each cache line written may also require a read-for-ownership if not all bytes in the line are written, but since the interior is mostly contiguous along z, most 128-byte cache lines will be fully written (398 elements along z, 398*8=3184 bytes, with 128-byte lines = ~25 full lines per row). The boundary elements (iz=0 and iz=399) are not written by this kernel, so some partial cache lines exist at the edges. The write traffic is approximately 504,358,336 bytes.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The first invocation is the first call to calculateForce inside the while loop at t=0. The OpenMP target kernel comes from `teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)` over 400*400*400 = 64,000,000 logical iterations, so the block/team size is constrained to 256 threads; the exact team count is runtime-chosen, and absent runtime/SASS details I use the defensible estimate grid.x = ceil(64,000,000 / 256) = 250,000 with y=z=1.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: `thread_limit(256)` directly constrains the OpenMP team thread count for this offloaded collapsed loop. For a 1-D flattened iteration space, the most defensible CUDA-style block shape estimate is 256x1x1.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: All arithmetic in this kernel is in `double`, not float or half. Therefore there are no source-level FP16 or FP32 operations in the first invocation.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: There are 64,000,000 total collapsed iterations, but only the interior points execute the heavy path: 398^3 = 63,044,792 points; the boundary points 64,000,000 - 63,044,792 = 955,208 only store zeros. Per interior point, GradientX/Y/Z cost 2 flops each (sub+div) = 6; `sqGphi` costs 5 mul/add flops; `c=16*W0*epsilon` costs 2; `w=Wn(...)` includes `An`: conditionally true for almost all interior points on the initialized sphere field, and then `An` costs 32 flops (including the expanded SQ macros, adds, muls, divs) plus 1 multiply in Wn = 33; `w2=w*w` costs 1; each `dFunc` call takes 24 flops on the nonzero path and is called 3 times = 72; each of Fx/Fy/Fz assignment costs 5 flops, totaling 15. That gives 134 FP64 flops per interior point, plus 0 on the boundary else-path, for 63,044,792 * 134 = 8,447,,? specifically 8,447,? 63,044,792*134 = 8,448,002,128 FP64 flops. This is source-level counting and excludes any extra lowered helper instructions from OpenMP/runtime or division implementations.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The kernel source uses only double-precision values and constants. Without SASS evidence of compiler-inserted packed half instructions, the defensible FP16 count is zero.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For interior points, the kernel reads only `phi` from global memory: GradientX/Y/Z each read two neighbor doubles, so 6 double loads = 48 B per interior iteration; outputs are write-only and scalar parameters are uniform kernel arguments. The unique `phi` footprint of the whole 400^3 array is 64,000,000 doubles = 512,000,000 B, which far exceeds the 40 MB L2, so reuse is not retained globally; a first-invocation source-level DRAM estimate is therefore dominated by total streaming loads, 63,044,792 * 48 = 3,026,150,016 B.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Every one of the 64,000,000 logical iterations writes one double each to Fx, Fy, and Fz: interior points write computed values and boundary points write 0.0, for 3 stores * 8 B = 24 B per iteration. The total unique output footprint is 3 * 64,000,000 * 8 = 1,536,000,000 B, far larger than the 40 MB L2, so these write-back lines must be evicted during the invocation; a defensible DRAM-write estimate is therefore the full output footprint.

prediction.blockSz_explanation: `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)` constrains the OpenMP team thread count, and the SASS uses `tid.x` with per-CTA iteration chunks of 256 (`ctaid.x << 8` plus lane/local thread handling), confirming 256 threads per block. prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Source-level arithmetic is entirely in double precision; however SASS shows several FP32 helper instructions executing on the taken path: three `FFMA R0, RZ, ...` zero/sign materializations in the main kernel (one per Laplacian axis division) and, for each taken call to `__cuda_sm20_div_rn_f64_full`, two `FSETP` comparisons plus one `MUFU.RCP64H`. prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Per logical iteration, the source computes `uold + 0.5*(phinew-phiold) + dt*D*Laplacian(uold,...)`. prediction.gridSz_explanation: The first invocation is the first call to calculateForce inside the while loop at t=0. The OpenMP target region uses collapse(3) over 400^3 = 64,000,000 logical iterations with thread_limit(256); the SASS shows CTAID.X compared against 0x3d08f and a 256-thread block (R60 shifted by 0x100), implying a runtime launch of 0x3d090 = 250,000 CTAs in x and 256 threads per CTA, exactly covering 64,000,000 logical iterations.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The source has thread_limit(256), and the SASS uses block base index = CTAID.X << 8 plus thread index, confirming 256 threads per CTA. No y/z thread dimensions are used.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: There is no source-level FP32 arithmetic in the kernel body; all user computations are in double precision. The SASS does contain a few FFMA/FSETP/HFMA2 helper instructions associated with control/division setup, but these are not FP32 floating-point operations contributing to the kernel’s modeled numerical work, so the defensible FP32 count is zero.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: The kernel executes 64,000,000 threads once each; 62,726,472 interior threads take the compute path and 1,273,528 boundary threads only store zeros. Using the executed SASS/source math for the interior path gives about 106 FP64 FLOPs for the three gradients, sqGphi, c, w/Wn/An, w2, three dFunc calls, and three output expressions; each gradient/division is counted from the lowered reciprocal/Newton/divide sequence visible in SASS, yielding 6.649005032e9 FP64 FLOPs total, while boundary threads perform no FP64 arithmetic.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The source uses no half-precision data, but the SASS shows compiler-emitted HFMA2 instructions used for constant/zero materialization and reciprocal-seed setup. Counting executed HFMA2s on the taken path gives 5 such instructions for every thread plus 3 additional HFMA2s on the interior path; at 4 FLOPs each, that is 20 FLOPs/thread for all 64,000,000 threads plus 12 FLOPs/interior-thread for 62,726,472 threads, totaling 2,032,717,664 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each interior point loads phi at its six direct neighbors: x±1, y±1, z±1, seen as six LDG.E.64 operations in SASS; boundary points do not load phi. The unique phi footprint touched by all interior iterations is the entire 400^3 array, 64,000,000 doubles = 512,000,000 bytes, and this fits easily in the 40 MB L2 only poorly (it is much larger), so the first-invocation DRAM read is well-approximated by that unique streamed footprint rather than 6 loads per interior point.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Every logical iteration writes exactly one double to each of Fx, Fy, and Fz, so the unique output footprint is 3 × 64,000,000 doubles = 1,536,000,000 bytes. These writes stream over 1.536 GB, far exceeding the 40 MB L2, so dirty lines will be evicted during the kernel and essentially the full unique store footprint reaches DRAM in the first invocation.

However, the SASS shows 9 LDG.E.64 instructions per thread iteration: 3 for uold x-neighbors (at offsets +0x271c88, +0xc88, +0x139488 which are +/-DATAYSIZE*DATAZSIZE*8 and center), 2 for uold y-neighbors (+0x13a108, +0x138808 = +/-DATAZSIZE*8), 2 for uold z-neighbors (+0x139490, +0x139480 = +/-8), and 2 for phinew and phiold (from the address computation using different base pointers). Actually looking more carefully: there are 9 LDG instructions total.

The unique data footprint: uold = 400*400*400*8 = 512MB, phinew = 512MB, phiold = 512MB. Total unique read footprint ~1.5GB. The L2 cache is 50MB, so most data will come from DRAM. With stencil reuse in L2, the effective DRAM read is approximately the unique footprint: uold (512MB) + phinew (398^3*8 ≈ 504MB but accessed as part of 512MB array) + phiold (similar). Total unique read ≈ 3 * 512MB = 1,536MB = 1,610,612,736 bytes. But only interior points are accessed for phinew/phiold, and stencil accesses for uold overlap significantly. Effective DRAM reads ≈ 3 * 400*400*400*8 = 1,536,000,000 bytes.

prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The swapGrid kernel reads from two arrays: cnew and cold. Each array has 400×400×400 = 64,000,000 double elements = 512,000,000 bytes. prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The swapGrid kernel writes to both cnew and cold arrays. Each array has 64,000,000 doubles = 512,000,000 bytes. Since this is 1 GB and the L2 cache is only 50 MB, the vast majority of written cache lines will be evicted to DRAM during the kernel execution. prediction.gridSz_explanation: The first invocation of the target kernel is the first call to thermalEquation inside the while loop at t=0. The OpenMP target region is `teams distribute parallel for collapse(3) thread_limit(256)` over ix,iy,iz with bounds 1..398 in each dimension, so there are 398^3 = 63,044,792 logical iterations; LLVM OpenMP offload fixes the team/thread geometry at runtime, but the defensible estimate is 256 threads per team and enough teams to cover all collapsed iterations once, giving ceil(63,044,792/256)=246,269 teams in x and 1 in y,z.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The directive explicitly specifies `thread_limit(256)`, which constrains the CUDA block size/team size for the generated OpenMP kernel. No other clause suggests a multidimensional thread geometry, so the best estimate is a 1D block of 256 threads.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: The kernel operates entirely on `double` values and constants; there are no half- or single-precision data types or arithmetic in source. Without SASS there is no basis to infer compiler-generated FP16/FP32 helper arithmetic for this simple stencil expression, so both are taken as zero.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Each executed iteration computes `uold + 0.5*(phinew-phiold) + dt*D*Laplacian(...)`. The Laplacian does three second derivatives, each costing 1 multiply for `2.0*u`, 2 adds/subtracts in the numerator, and 1 divide by squared spacing = 4 FP64 ops, plus 2 adds to sum phixx+phiyy+phizz, for 14 ops total; outside that, `phinew-phiold` (1), multiply by 0.5 (1), `dt*D` (1), multiply by Laplacian (1), add to uold (1), and final add (1) give 6 more, so 20 FP64 ops per interior point. The loop covers 398^3 = 63,044,792 interior points on the first invocation, yielding 63,044,792 * 20 = 1,260,895,840 FP64 FLOPs.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The source uses only double-precision arrays and constants in this kernel, with no half-precision arithmetic or data movement. In the absence of SASS, no compiler-generated FP16 instructions are defensibly attributable to this stencil kernel.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For each interior point, source-level loads are `uold[ix][iy][iz]`, `phinew[ix][iy][iz]`, `phiold[ix][iy][iz]`, and the 7-point Laplacian on `uold` (center plus six neighbors) = 10 double loads per point, or 80 B. The interior iteration space is 398^3 = 63,044,792 points, so total streaming read traffic is 5,043,583,360 B; the unique footprint touched is about 512 MB for uold plus about 512 MB each for phinew and phiold, far exceeding the 5 MB L2, so reuse is negligible at DRAM scale and the total-load estimate is appropriate.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each interior point writes exactly one double to `unew[ix][iy][iz]`, so the unique and total store footprint for the first invocation is 63,044,792 * 8 = 504,358,336 B. Because this write footprint alone is much larger than the 5 MB L2 cache, dirty lines cannot remain resident for the whole kernel and will be evicted to DRAM during the invocation, so DRAM writes are well approximated by the full store footprint.

**Boundary threads:** These are threads where ix==0, ix==399, iy==0, iy==399, iz==0, or iz==399. They execute `Fx[ix][iy][iz] = 0.0; Fy[ix][iy][iz] = 0.0; Fz[ix][iy][iz] = 0.0;` — no FP64 ops (stores of constants).

Number of boundary points: 400×400×400 - 398×398×398 = 64,000,000 - 63,044,792 = 955,208 boundary threads.
Number of interior threads: 63,044,792.

**Interior thread FP64 operations:**

1. `GradientX`: phi[x+1][y][z] - phi[x-1][y][z] → 1 sub; / (2.0*dx) → 1 mul (2.0*dx is constant-folded), 1 div or mul by reciprocal = 1 op. Total: 2 FP64 ops.
2. `GradientY`: same → 2 FP64 ops.
3. `GradientZ`: same → 2 FP64 ops.
4. `sqGphi = SQ(phix) + SQ(phiy) + SQ(phiz)`: 3 muls + 2 adds = 5 ops.
5. `c = 16.0 * W0 * epsilon`: W0=1.0, epsilon=0.07, so c = 16.0*1.0*0.07. This could be constant-folded by the compiler since all are passed as scalar arguments that are constants. But conservatively, 2 muls = 2 ops. However, the compiler with -O3 will likely fold this. Let me count conservatively as 0 (constant folded at compile time since they're function parameters but known constants... actually they're runtime values passed to the function). So 2 muls.
6. `Wn` calls `An`:
   - `An(phix, phiy, phiz, epsilon)`: For the likely case (non-zero gradients):
     - `SQ(phix)*SQ(phix)` = phix^4: 2 muls (phix*phix, then result*result) = 2
     - `SQ(phiy)*SQ(phiy)` = 2 muls
     - `SQ(phiz)*SQ(phiz)` = 2 muls
     - Sum of 4th powers: 2 adds
     - `SQ(phix)+SQ(phiy)+SQ(phiz)`: already computed as sqGphi, compiler may reuse = 0 (or 5 if not reused). Likely reused with -O3.
     - `(SQ(phix)+SQ(phiy)+SQ(phiz))*(SQ(phix)+SQ(phiy)+SQ(phiz))`: 1 mul
     - Division: 1 div
     - `1.0 - 3.0*epsilon`: 1 mul + 1 sub = 2 (but could be constant folded since epsilon is a parameter... it's a runtime value though)
     - `4.0*epsilon`: 1 mul
     - `4.0*epsilon/(1.0-3.0*epsilon)`: 1 div
     - Multiply by the ratio: 1 mul
     - `1.0 + ...`: 1 add
     - `(1.0-3.0*epsilon) * (1.0 + ...)`: 1 mul
     Total An: ~2+2+2+2+1+1+2+1+1+1+1+1 = 17 ops (but some subexpressions like 1-3*epsilon and 4*epsilon/(1-3*epsilon) may be hoisted out of the per-thread computation since epsilon is loop-invariant). With -O3, `1-3*epsilon`, `4*epsilon/(1-3*epsilon)` are loop-invariant and will be hoisted. So An per thread: phix^4 (can reuse SQ(phix)=phix*phix already computed, so 1 mul for phix^2*phix^2), phiy^4 (1 mul), phiz^4 (1 mul), sum of 4th powers (2 adds), sqGphi^2 (1 mul), division (1 div), multiply by hoisted constant (1 mul), add 1.0 (1 add), multiply by hoisted (1-3*eps) (1 mul). That's about 10 ops.
   - `Wn = W0 * An(...)`: 1 mul. But W0=1.0, compiler might optimize away. Count 1 mul conservatively.
   - Total Wn: ~11 ops.
7. `w2 = SQ(w)`: 1 mul.
8. For Fx: `w2 * phix`: 1 mul. `dFunc(phix,phiy,phiz)`: 
   - `l*l*l*(SQ(m)+SQ(n))`: l^3 = 2 muls, m^2 = 1 mul, n^2 = 1 mul, sum = 1 add, product = 1 mul = 6 ops
   - `l*(SQ(m)*SQ(m)+SQ(n)*SQ(n))`: m^4 = 1 mul (reuse m^2), n^4 = 1 mul (reuse n^2), sum = 1 add, l*sum = 1 mul = 4 ops
   - Subtraction: 1 sub
   - Denominator: `(SQ(l)+SQ(m)+SQ(n))^2` = sqGphi^2 (already computed in An) = 0 new ops if reused, else 1 mul
   - Division: 1 div
   - Total dFunc: ~12 ops (conservatively, some reuse possible)
   - `sqGphi * w * c * dFunc(...)`: 3 muls
   - `w2*phix + ...`: 1 add
   - Total for Fx line: 1 + 12 + 3 + 1 = 17 ops
9. Fy line: similar dFunc call with different argument order. dFunc(phiy,phiz,phix): ~12 ops + 3 muls + 1 add = 16 ops (w2*phiy reuses w2)
10. Fz line: similar: ~16 ops

metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_read_explanation:
The kernel reads from `phi` array and writes to `Fx`, `Fy`, `Fz` arrays. Each array is 400×400×400 doubles = 512,000,000 bytes.

For reads: Each interior thread reads 7 values from phi (phi[x][y][z], phi[x±1][y][z], phi[x][y±1][z], phi[x][y][z±1]). The unique read footprint is the entire phi array = 400×400×400×8 = 512,000,000 bytes. This is 512 MB, which is much larger than the 6 MB L2 cache, so essentially all reads will come from DRAM.

The total unique read footprint is 512 MB for phi. Due to stencil access patterns with neighbor accesses, there will be some L2 cache reuse for overlapping accesses between nearby threads in the same warp/block, but since the working set (512 MB) vastly exceeds L2 (6 MB), most data will need to be fetched from DRAM. The actual DRAM read traffic may be close to the unique footprint of ~512 MB, possibly slightly more due to cache line granularity effects but also slightly less due to some L2 reuse within streaming windows.

DRAM bytes read ≈ 512,000,000 bytes.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes to three arrays: Fx, Fy, Fz, each of size 400×400×400×8 = 512,000,000 bytes. Every thread writes exactly one element to each of Fx, Fy, Fz (either computed values for interior or 0.0 for boundary). Total unique write footprint = 3 × 512,000,000 = 1,536,000,000 bytes = 1.536 GB. This vastly exceeds the 6 MB L2 cache, so virtually all writes will be evicted to DRAM during the kernel execution. The streaming write pattern means cache lines are written and then evicted as new data arrives. DRAM bytes written ≈ 1,536,000,000 bytes.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel `boundaryConditionsU` iterates over a collapsed 3D loop of 400×400×400 = 64,000,000 elements with `thread_limit(256)`. The OpenMP runtime on clang for NVIDIA targets typically launches ceil(64000000/256) = 250000 teams. So gridSz = [250000, 1, 1].
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The `thread_limit(256)` clause directly sets the block size to 256 threads. So blockSz = [256, 1, 1].
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: No single-precision floating point operations are performed in this kernel. All operations use double precision. There may be a small number of compiler-generated FP32 instructions (e.g., for constant materialization), but from source analysis, the count is 0.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: The kernel `boundaryConditionsU` applies boundary conditions to a 400×400×400 array. For boundary elements (where ix==0, ix==399, iy==0, iy==399, iz==0, or iz==399), it writes `-delta` which requires a FP64 negation operation. The parameter `delta` is 0.8, and `-delta` is computed as a negation. Let's count the boundary elements: The total number of boundary elements where at least one index is 0 or 399 is: total - interior = 64000000 - 398×398×398 = 64000000 - 63044792 = 955208. Each boundary thread performs one FP64 negation of delta to produce -delta. Interior threads (63044792) perform no FP64 ops. However, the compiler likely precomputes `-delta` as a constant (it's a kernel parameter that doesn't change), so the negation may be done once or folded into a constant. If the compiler passes `-delta` as a precomputed value, there are 0 FP64 FLOPs. But conservatively, the negation of delta is 1 FP64 op per boundary thread = 955208 FP64 ops. Actually, looking more carefully, `-delta` is likely computed once and stored in a register, not per-thread. The compiler will negate delta once. So effectively 1 FP64 FLOP for the negation, but since each thread that hits a boundary branch just stores the pre-negated value, the per-thread FP64 work is 0. The most likely scenario is 0 FP64 FLOPs since the compiler precomputes -delta.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: No half-precision floating point operations are present in this kernel. The kernel only deals with double-precision data. There may be a small number of compiler-generated FP16 instructions for constant materialization (e.g., HFMA2 for zero initialization), but this is uncertain without SASS. Estimating 0 conservatively.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel reads from `unew` array only for interior elements that don't match any boundary condition (they fall through all if/else-if branches without writing). However, looking at the code more carefully: the kernel only writes to boundary elements and does nothing for interior elements. There are no reads from the array at all - the kernel only writes constant values (-delta) to boundary positions. The only "read" is the scalar parameter `delta`. The compiler may still generate loads for the loop index computation, but no array reads. So DRAM bytes read is essentially 0 for array data. However, the OpenMP runtime may read some small bookkeeping data. Estimating 0 bytes read from DRAM for this kernel's actual work.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes -delta (8 bytes each, double precision) to all boundary elements of the 400×400×400 array. The number of boundary elements is 400×400×400 - 398×398×398 = 64000000 - 63044792 = 955208 elements. Each write is 8 bytes, so total write footprint = 955208 × 8 = 7,641,664 bytes ≈ 7.3 MB. The L2 cache is 50 MB, so this entire write footprint fits in L2. Since the L2 is write-back, these dirty cache lines will remain in L2 and not be flushed to DRAM during this kernel invocation. Therefore DRAM bytes written ≈ 0.
